articles.title: How to Tell If Your Linux Server Has Been Hacked: Warning Signs and First Steps
articles.excerpt: Most server compromises don't announce themselves. There's no ransom note and no defaced homepage. Instead there's a creeping sense that something isn't right: the load average is higher than it shoul…
articles.body: Most server compromises don't announce themselves. There's no ransom note and no defaced homepage. Instead there's a creeping sense that something isn't right: the load average is higher than it should be, outbound mail is bouncing, or there's a login you don't recognise. If you run a Linux server, whether it hosts websites, email or an application, it helps to know what the early signs look like and what to do about them. This guide covers both. Why compromises often go unnoticed Attackers who get into a server usually want to stay there. A quietly compromised machine can send spam, mine cryptocurrency, host phishing pages or act as a stepping stone to other systems. All of that works best if the owner doesn't notice.
articles.author: William Smith

articles.title: Run Your Own Vaultwarden Password Manager on a VPS with Docker
articles.excerpt: Password managers hold the keys to everything you own online, yet the hosted ones put that vault on someone else's servers and often lock useful features behind a subscription. If you'd rather keep co…
articles.body: Password managers hold the keys to everything you own online, yet the hosted ones put that vault on someone else's servers and often lock useful features behind a subscription. If you'd rather keep control of your own data, self-hosting is a realistic option, even on a small VPS. In this guide we build a private Vaultwarden server, a lightweight, Bitwarden-compatible backend, running in Docker. It is never exposed to the public internet and is reachable only through an SSH tunnel. We also add automatic daily backups and disable public sign-ups, so the only account on the server is yours. You get the polished Bitwarden apps and extensions, with a vault that lives on a machine you control. What you need A VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 (2 vCPU / 4 GB RAM is plenty).
articles.author: Артем Ахмадеев

articles.title: How to charge a subscription in an AI-built app and unlock features only for those who paid
articles.excerpt: The app the AI helped you build has users, and now you want to charge. The agent usually proposes wiring Stripe directly: products, checkout, a webhook endpoint, subscription state in your database, a…
articles.body: The app the AI helped you build has users, and now you want to charge. The agent usually proposes wiring Stripe directly: products, checkout, a webhook endpoint, subscription state in your database, a check on every screen. It works, but those pieces have to agree with each other. And the classic mistake of an app built in a hurry is hiding the paid button in the frontend while the server route stays open. This is the path with Payments, from the Infrastructure line (by Ciro Cesar Maciel, who writes this). The pieces, in one sentence A project holds gateways ; each gateway holds plans ; a customer subscribes to a plan and gets the features linked to it. The app never asks "which plan is this user on?". It asks "does this user have advanced-reports ?".
articles.author: Ciro Cesar Maciel

articles.title: Proximal Policy Optimization: Why Clipping the Update Beats Trusting the Gradient
articles.excerpt: Policy gradient methods have a seductive simplicity. Collect trajectories, estimate which actions helped, and shift the policy toward those actions. The problem is that the same simplicity makes them…
articles.body: Policy gradient methods have a seductive simplicity. Collect trajectories, estimate which actions helped, and shift the policy toward those actions. The problem is that the same simplicity makes them fragile. One bad update can move the policy so far that the data it collects next is useless, and recovery takes a long time. Proximal Policy Optimization, or PPO, is the practical answer to that fragility. It does not introduce a new learning objective from first principles. It takes the ordinary policy gradient objective, adds a cheap guardrail that stops the policy from moving too far in a single step, and thereby turns a method that often diverges into one that reliably improves.

articles.title: Frontend Development Internship: A Practical Starting Point for Beginners
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: This article is written by the MaMo Technolabs team, which offers a frontend development internship in Vadodara. The tips apply to any internship. If you’re a beginner, a frontend developm…
articles.body: Disclosure: This article is written by the MaMo Technolabs team, which offers a frontend development internship in Vadodara. The tips apply to any internship. If you’re a beginner, a frontend development internship is a practical place to start. Your first tasks probably won’t be “build a whole app”. They’ll be smaller and more realistic. Here are tasks interns commonly meet, and how to approach them. Task 1: Fix a Layout Bug A card overflows on mobile. Check the box model and use developer tools. A fixed width of 400px breaks on small screens. A better approach is to set the width to 100% and add a max-width of 400px. Task 2: Make a Button Accessible Use a real button element, not a clickable div. Buttons work with the keyboard by default.

articles.title: Jobs That Fade, Jobs That Emerge: What the Labour Market Looks Like Up to 2030
articles.excerpt: Originally published at scouthub.dev. Some jobs will shrink a lot before 2030: data entry clerks, bank tellers, postal clerks. Others will grow fast: data and AI specialists, but also work that has no…
articles.body: Originally published at scouthub.dev . Some jobs will shrink a lot before 2030: data entry clerks, bank tellers, postal clerks. Others will grow fast: data and AI specialists, but also work that has nothing to do with screens, such as farming, delivery, construction and nursing. And the most important number is not about jobs at all: employers expect about 39% of the skills they need to change in these years [1]. In short: The forecast: 170 million new jobs, 92 million displaced, a net gain of 78 million [2]. Most declining roles are routine: data entry, clerical work, checkout counters [3]. Growing roles come in two kinds: advanced tech, and human or manual work that is hard to replace [4]. What protects a person is not a job title but the ability to learn again.

articles.title: YouTube captions in Postgres: preserve the revision your answer cited
articles.excerpt: Your answer still cites the video. The transcript behind that citation has changed, and your upsert has helpfully deleted the version you embedded. You discover this while investigating an answer some…
articles.body: Your answer still cites the video. The transcript behind that citation has changed, and your upsert has helpfully deleted the version you embedded. You discover this while investigating an answer someone challenged. The recording is available. The evidence isn't. A video ID identifies a recording, not a transcript revision. The Actor processes duplicate video IDs once, but language selection and collection paths determine which text comes back. Deduplicating collection doesn't preserve evidence. Choose what your citation promises For timestamped citations, preserve text and segment boundaries together. A text-only hash misses timing changes, even when those changes move the passage your answer points to. Use Node with ES modules, apify-client , zod , and pg .

articles.body: In recent years, Google has made impressive strides in software accessibility. From real-time captions and AI-powered vision tools to refined high-contrast display options across Android, the company frequently touts its commitment to creating technology that works for everyone. With the release of its 2026 Fitbit lineup , Google has pushed this mission even further, introducing a suite of features aimed at lowering price barriers, streamlining health tracking, and making health insights simpler to understand. By almost every traditional metric, Fitbit wearables are more accessible today than they have ever been. Yet, for millions of people worldwide who use wheelchairs, that promise of inclusivity quickly hits a wall.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 just reached a light-day in space, but Voyager 2 won't do the same until 2035, due to speed choices made throughout their 50-year missions.
articles.body: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?
articles.author: Elizabeth Howell

articles.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
articles.excerpt: The British company Foundational thinks its laser-reflecting tech can help humanity fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.
articles.body: A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors.
articles.author: Elizabeth Howell

articles.title: Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova
articles.excerpt: Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.
articles.body: Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova. Most of us know the origin story of black holes , or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole. However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth.
articles.author: Robert Lea

articles.title: ULA lost a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying 40 Amazon satellites 10 minutes after launch — but the failure began just after liftoff
articles.excerpt: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket failed during its launch on Sunday (Nov. 15) because of an issue with its first-stage booster, according to the company.
articles.body: The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17). That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement. "While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update .
articles.author: Mike Wall

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface. Here's how it helped Apollo astronauts.
articles.body: On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface. Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff. First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off. Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11 .
